default_exit._why: one exit for every family so rules compete on the same footing; the owner will decide the demo stop/take-profit later and this block changes then (a change = a new screen run, its variants counted again)
default_exit._fills: signal at the close of bar t; market order at the open of the 1-minute bar that starts at t's close (+ slippage); every 1-minute bar from the entry minute on: stop first (fills at the stop or the gap open, - slippage), then the target (a limit: needs a trade 1 tick through, fills at the target); time exit at the open of the first minute at or after entry + max_hold_min; flat at the session's flatten time; one position at a time; at most max_entries_per_session entries per session

E-278.title: Dense-profile micro-break fade
E-278.hypothesis: A close beyond the recent high/low that lands in a price zone where a large share of today's earlier volume already traded is breaking into accepted inventory: the holders from that zone (and the passive orders that made it a high-volume node) sell into the up-break and buy the down-break, so the small breaker is faded.

E-279.title: Round-number cross follow (stop cascade)
E-279.hypothesis: Stop-loss buy orders cluster just above round numbers and stop-loss sells just below; a close through a round level triggers that cluster, and the executed stops are market orders that push the price further (Osler's price cascades), so follow the close through the round number.

E-280.title: High-low spread-regime micro-break fade
E-280.hypothesis: When the Corwin-Schultz high-low spread estimate over the last window runs well above its 20-session norm, bar ranges are made mostly of bid-ask bouncing between liquidity providers rather than of information; a 10-minute high/low break then is the bounce reaching the far quote, which the providers lean back, so fade.

E-281.title: Expanding-range run follow
E-281.hypothesis: Consecutive same-colour bars whose ranges grow each bar, ending with a bar of at least normal range for the minute, show an aggressive parent order accelerating while market makers widen and pull quotes; the urgency is not spent at the bar close, so follow the run's direction.

E-282.title: Intraday head-and-shoulders neckline break follow
E-282.hypothesis: Three swing highs with a higher middle and roughly level shoulders mean the last push failed below the head; chart traders who see the pattern sell the close through the neckline and the longs from the right shoulder have stops just under it, so the neckline break is followed (inverse pattern for longs).

E-283.title: Multi-session-trend micro-break follow
E-283.hypothesis: When yesterday closed above the average price of the last several sessions, swing holders are long and positioned to add; intraday breaks in that direction are joined by their adds and by short covering, while breaks against it meet their dip-buying, so follow only breaks aligned with the multi-session trend.

E-284.title: Half-gap level hold
E-284.hypothesis: On a meaningful opening gap, gap-fade traders take profit at the half-gap (midpoint of yesterday's close and today's open) and gap-continuation traders buy it; a bar that reaches the half-gap and closes back on the gap side shows that interest absorbing the fill, so trade back toward the open.

E-285.title: Camarilla H3/L3 fade, H4/L4 break
E-285.hypothesis: Camarilla levels (yesterday's close +/- 1.1 x range / 4 and / 2) are a published day-trader map: users sell the first touch of H3 that closes back below and buy L3, but chase a close beyond H4/L4; their shared orders make those reactions self-fulfilling at the level.

E-286.title: Heavy-opening-auction day micro-break fade
E-286.hypothesis: A session whose opening bar trades much more than its usual volume priced the overnight information in the auction itself; the rest of the day has no informed parent order left to work and is run by responsive liquidity providers, so after the first half hour short-term breaks are faded.

E-287.title: Three-line-break reversal follow
E-287.hypothesis: On a three-line-break chart a reversal needs a close beyond the extreme of the last N same-colour lines, i.e. the whole recent leg is undone on closing prices; the leg's late entrants are then under water and exit while the chart's users enter the new direction, so follow the reversal after a leg of at least N lines.
